title: Grassfire: dry meadow vs wet meadow
question: You asked for moisture vs dryness to play a role. Does this read as it playing a role — one meadow carries the fire, the other refuses it?
context_md:
**The same sward, grown once, burnt twice.** A dry meadow cannot be *grown* — unplanted soil fills up as it goes — so both arms grow on identical ground and the bed is reset 600 frames before the ignition. Identical fuel, one number different: how wet the ground under it is.

**Why this changed anything.** The moisture term has existed for two milestones and measured as doing nothing. It was not too weak. Its input — the diffused humidity at the cell — reads **exactly 0.000 at 96.8% of fuel cells, at every ground wetness from the wilting point to saturated**. A field block containing a plant cell is marked blocked, and a blocked block never diffuses, so *the presence of fuel is what makes a block read bone dry*. Over the whole dry-to-saturated span the old term moved ignition by 5%.

It now reads the wetness of the ground itself, which comes out 0.00 / 0.18 / 0.62 / 1.00 at the fuel for the four beds, exactly as it should.

**Swept, not one run:** 12 different swards (4 founder counts x 3 weather windows), each burnt at three wetnesses. At field capacity **no sward lost more than 8% of itself**; when dry, **5 of the 12 burnt out entirely**. Front distance: 67-489 cells dry, never past 74 damp.

What I would like your eye on rather than the numbers: whether the wet arm reads as *the meadow refusing to burn*, or just as a fire that fizzled.
